title: What Epidemiological Studies Tell Us About Depression Among Black Populations?
content: Depression among Black patients is shaped by the interaction of clinical symptoms, cultural meanings, social conditions, and experiences of care. This narrative review examines evidence among African American and other Black populations, including Black–White comparisons and within-Black differences, on symptom presentation, measurement, persistence, disability, comorbidity, and social and cultural correlates, across the United States and selected Canadian, European, and African settings. Targeted searches identified population surveys, clinical studies, psychometric investigations, qualitative research, intervention trials, and relevant reviews. James S. Jackson's research agenda provides a starting point: understanding comparatively favorable findings in the context of historical and continuing adversity. Several United States surveys report lower lifetime prevalence of interview-defined major depression among Black than White adults, while symptom scales often indicate greater depressive burden among Black adults. This Black–White mental health paradox varies by outcome and population; some studies identify greater persistence and disability among Black adults with depression. Studies of hope, positive affect, coping resources, and physical health suggest that the correlates of depression may also differ across groups, although no single mechanism explains the pattern. Evidence on distinctive symptom presentation is mixed. Some studies identify Black–White differences or within-Black variation in bodily symptoms, self-criticism, or interpersonal experiences, whereas others find substantial similarity after accounting for severity and social or medical conditions. Psychiatric and physical comorbidity among Black adults with depression varies across samples, including in comparisons with White adults. Associations of depressive symptoms or MDD with smoking, disease self-management, self-rated health, inflammation, and mortality differ across studies and populations; colorism, trauma, sexuality, gender, and migration further identify within-Black heterogeneity. The review examines associations of discrimination, financial strain, employment conditions, family relationships, and gendered expectations with depressive symptoms, MDD, and treatment use among Black populations. Studies of Black populations also examine political representation and insurance expansion in relation to self-reported mental health, and loneliness, personality, and distinct church-based relationships in relation to depressive symptoms or MDD. Social support, religious involvement, mastery, and socioeconomic resources are associated with depressive symptoms or MDD in several studies, with variation across measures, social positions, and national settings. Studies also identify disparities in medication initiation and selection, communication, continuity, and care quality; stigma, discrimination in care, and medical debt are relevant to treatment access and experience. Cultural assessment and accessible, sustained depression care may improve recognition and engagement. Future research should distinguish symptom burden from diagnosed disorder, assess longitudinal course directly, and avoid treating Black identity as a single cultural or biological category.
